solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Before head of committee, recommend moving folder for infant (9)

indicatorNotes.Before: 'Before' means coming earlier, so the piece for 'recommend moving' is written ahead of the committee's head.

blocks.note: to push a product is to promote it and get it moving
the person who presides over a committee

annotation.surface: A meeting where someone keeps pressing to have a file moved before the chair sees it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head of committee' looks like an instruction to take the letter C; here it is the whole person. The 'folder' is not a file but something that folds.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description by function: this child's seat on wheels folds flat, so it is a folder for an infant.

entries.clue: Before party, say churchwarden started to speak (5,2)

indicatorNotes.Before: 'Before' means coming earlier, so the churchwarden's piece is written ahead of the party.

blocks.note: a churchwarden is a long-stemmed clay tobacco pipe; 'say' marks it as an example
the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

annotation.surface: A church official is about to speak up at a parish party.
annotation.walkthrough: The churchwarden looks like a parish officer; it is a kind of pipe. The DUP is a Northern Irish political party.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to pipe up is to begin speaking, often unexpectedly, like a pipe suddenly sounding.

entries.clue: Profit from currency makes going easier when travelling (11)

indicatorNotes.when travelling: Travelling means moving from place to place, so the letters move out of their order.

annotation.surface: A traveller notes that having the local money makes the trip smoother.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about spending currency abroad, which sits close to the real subject: the money a state makes by issuing coins and notes.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical term: the gap between the face value of money and what it costs to produce is profit to the issuer.

entries.clue: River is treacly, dead in places (5)

indicatorNotes.in places: The answer is found in places, that is, in parts of the words, spread across two of them.

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of 'treacly' and the start of 'dead'

annotation.surface: A polluted river is sticky and lifeless in stretches.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface of a dirty river hides the name of a real one; it runs through Glasgow.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is a named river in Scotland.

entries.clue: A peremptory refusal by one African people (7)

blocks.note: a curt 'shall not!', with the apostrophe dropped

annotation.surface: One member of an African people curtly refuses something.
annotation.walkthrough: Grids ignore apostrophes, so the contraction goes in as five plain letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain name: this is a people of Ghana, in West Africa, historically a powerful kingdom.

entries.clue: Have regrets? That’s the French way (3)

blocks.note: an old-fashioned verb for being sorry about something
the French word for a street, as in Paris addresses

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether regret is a peculiarly French habit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Way' is a road, as in a street name, not a manner of doing things.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: an English verb for regretting, and the French noun for a street, which is a way.

entries.clue: Abnormally short street, one lacking smallest bit of illumination (7)

indicatorNotes.lacking: To lack something is to be without it, so UNITED goes without its I.

blocks.note: united = made one, as in 'we stand as one'
the first letter of 'illumination', removed from UNITED to leave UNTED

annotation.surface: A short street is poorly lit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One' here is not I or A but the adjective UNITED.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: growth that has been held back leaves something abnormally short.

entries.clue: Part poet’s hair (9)

blocks.note: a part or section, as in 'the east side of town'
Robert Burns, Scotland's national poet; the 's joins him to the definition

annotation.surface: Instructions to part a poet's hair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Part' reads as a verb for combing a parting; it is a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: these are a particular growth of hair down the sides of the face.

entries.clue: Country club, in absence of leader, really disorderly (6)

indicatorNotes.in absence of leader: The leader is the first letter, and its absence means it is taken away.

blocks.note: the United Nations, a club whose members are countries
truly = really; losing its leader T gives RULY

annotation.surface: A golf club's bar gets rowdy while the captain is away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country club' is the setter's playful name for the United Nations, not a golf club.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who will not obey rules is disorderly.

entries.clue: The Moor’s weakness: deserter — men, they gone runnin’! (3,5-4,7)

indicatorNotes.runnin’: Running away scatters things, so the letters of the fodder are scattered into a new order.

annotation.surface: A folksy cry that the deserters have all run off.
annotation.walkthrough: The Moor is Othello, whose downfall is jealousy; Iago warns him of it using this very phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary allusion: Shakespeare's name for jealousy, the flaw that destroys Othello the Moor.

entries.clue: Share in payout reversed Red Wall? (7)

indicatorNotes.reversed: Reversed means turned the other way, so RED is written backwards.

blocks.note: short for dividend, a shareholder's slice of the profits

annotation.surface: The 'Red Wall' of Labour seats changing hands at an election.
annotation.walkthrough: The Red Wall is the UK press name for Labour's old heartland seats in the north of England. The question mark flags a definition by example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a wall is one kind of thing that separates one space from another.

entries.clue: No weaknesses at motorway rest area: one doesn’t want to spend a penny (5)

annotation.definition: one doesn’t want to spend a penny

indicatorNotes.No: 'No weaknesses' means with the weaknesses gone, so their letters are removed.

blocks.note: M1 services, with the 1 written as I
vices are moral weaknesses; these letters come out

annotation.surface: A spotless motorway stop, and a traveller who won't pay to use the toilet.
annotation.walkthrough: The M1 is England's main motorway north from London. 'Spend a penny' is a British euphemism for using a toilet, which once cost a penny.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on an idiom: someone who hoards money hates spending even a penny, though the phrase usually means going to the toilet.

entries.clue: Imperious back’s brief force in struggle for ball (9)

indicatorNotes.brief: Brief means short, so the word is cut short by its last letter.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' places the preceding pieces inside the word for the struggle.

blocks.note: the back of a ship is its STERN; brief drops the N
F is the physics symbol for force
a maul is a rugby tussle for the ball; STERF goes in after MA

annotation.surface: A rugby full-back throws his weight around in a maul.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a rugby position beside 'struggle for ball'; it is the rear of a boat.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe someone who likes to command others.

entries.clue: Cheat chauffeur that goes round and round delivering Premium Bonds? (11)

annotation.definition: that goes round and round delivering Premium Bonds?

blocks.note: a chauffeur is someone paid to drive

annotation.surface: A crooked chauffeur drives round and round delivering savings certificates.
annotation.walkthrough: Premium Bonds are a UK government savings scheme with prize draws; here the phrase is reread as top-quality fixings.
annotation.definitionFit: A cheeky cryptic description: the tool turns round and round, driving in screws that make first-rate bonds.

entries.clue: Slightly unwell, like a guy perhaps (5)

blocks.note: British informal for feeling below par
a guy is a line that holds a tent or mast steady, so something like a guy resembles a cord

annotation.surface: Someone says a man looks a bit off-colour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Guy' reads as a man; it is a guy rope.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: British slang for poorly, and literally resembling the cord a guy is made of.

entries.clue: Naturalist’s help worked with tiny tree (5,3,5)

indicatorNotes.worked: Worked means shaped by effort, as clay is worked, so the letters are reshaped.

blocks.note: a small tree with white flowers and dark berries

annotation.surface: A naturalist's assistant has been tending a little tree.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay. 'Tiny' belongs with the fodder, not describing the tree.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the Roman author of the Natural History is a famous early naturalist.

entries.clue: Away from lake, what happens in autumn to earwig (9)

indicatorNotes.Away from: To be away from something is to be apart from it, so the lake's letter is taken out.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, removed from the front

annotation.surface: An insect's fate by a lake in autumn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Earwig' looks like the insect; it is a British verb meaning to listen in.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional synonym: in British slang, to earwig is to listen in secretly on others.

entries.clue: Prelate keeps a set of books similar to some poetry (7)

indicatorNotes.keeps: To keep is to hold on to, so the prelate holds the other pieces inside him.

blocks.note: a senior churchman; A and NT go in after D

annotation.surface: A churchman looks after a shelf of verse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set of books' is a crossword staple for OT or NT, the two Testaments of the Bible.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective from a name: resembling the poetry of Dante, author of the Divine Comedy.

entries.clue: Indistinct farm animal almost comes in close (7)

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost means not quite complete, so the last letter is dropped.
indicatorNotes.comes in: To come in is to enter, so the animal enters the word for close.

blocks.note: a farm animal, almost, gives BUL
close = near; BUL goes in after NE

annotation.surface: A bull wanders dimly into view nearby.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Close' reads as a verb, to shut; it is the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: like a nebula, a hazy cloud in space, so cloudy and indistinct.

entries.clue: Ache to see a new planet, presumably, and soon to depart (3,4,3,4,5)

annotation.definition2: Ache to see a new planet, presumably

blocks.clueFragment: Ache to see a new planet, presumably
blocks.note: someone who aches for another planet does not yearn for the one they live on
the idiom for someone near death

annotation.surface: A would-be space traveller eager to leave Earth.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half rereads 'long' as the verb, to yearn, rather than the adjective about time.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the idiom for someone close to dying, and literally not yearning for Earth.

entries.clue: Stamp out what the Cheshire Cat did (3,4)

blocks.note: a tool for stamping designs onto coins

annotation.surface: An order to crush whatever the Cheshire Cat got up to.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stamp out' looks like one phrase meaning destroy; it splits into two pieces. In Alice in Wonderland the Cheshire Cat fades until only its grin is left.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion: the Cheshire Cat gradually faded, the phrasal verb for a slow fade.

entries.clue: Appeasing is strangely a top priority (12)

indicatorNotes.strangely: Strangely means in an odd way, so the letters are arranged oddly.

annotation.surface: Someone oddly makes keeping others happy their number-one goal.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a remark about people-pleasing, which happens to sit right beside the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe what is meant to calm anger or win favour.

entries.clue: Popular addition to wedding dress going on (2,5)

blocks.note: the long trailing back of a bridal gown

annotation.surface: A fashionable extra for a bride's gown, and the preparations under way.
annotation.walkthrough: The formal phrase means under way, as in 'plans are in train'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: something in train is already in progress, going on.

entries.clue: Stable position that regularly limits blunder by American company (5,5)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken.
indicatorNotes.limits: To limit is to set bounds, so TA forms the boundary around ERR.
indicatorNotes.by: By means beside, so the company and American follow on.

blocks.note: to err is to make a mistake; it goes inside TA

annotation.surface: A US company's position holds firm despite a mistake.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stable position' sounds like business jargon; it is solid ground.
annotation.definitionFit: A Latin phrase: literally 'firm land', solid ground as opposed to sea or air, hence a stable place to stand.

entries.clue: End of quarrel as leader of school leaves hospital (9)

indicatorNotes.leaves: To leave is to depart, so the hospital's letter departs.

blocks.note: the head of Harrow, a famous English public school

annotation.surface: A headmaster's discharge from hospital ends a row.
annotation.walkthrough: A quarrel is also a square-headed crossbow bolt. 'Leader of school' looks like its first letter S; it is Harrow's headteacher.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on quarrel: the pointed tip is the end of a crossbow bolt.

entries.clue: To meet, career regularly around southern state (6)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken.
indicatorNotes.around: Around means surrounding, so AER surrounds the state.

blocks.note: New South Wales, an Australian state; it goes in after A

annotation.surface: A racer circles a southern US state to meet someone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Southern state' suggests Alabama or Georgia; it is in Australia, with 'South' in its very name.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in one sense: to answer a need or demand is to meet it.

entries.clue: Out of place, I sleep at back of hut (5)

indicatorNotes.back of: The back of a word is its end, so the last letter is taken.

annotation.surface: Someone out of their element dozes behind a shed.
annotation.walkthrough: Not to be confused with inept: this word means unsuitable rather than clumsy.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a remark that does not suit the occasion is out of place.

entries.clue: Isolated home recently found in south of France (9)

indicatorNotes.found in: Something found in a place is inside it, so LATE sits inside SUD.

blocks.note: the French word for south; LATE goes in after SU

annotation.surface: A remote house recently discovered in the south of France.
annotation.walkthrough: 'South of France' reads as the region; it asks for the French word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something shielded from outside influence is cut off, isolated.

entries.clue: Making decorative art, one boy put in identical copy (9)

indicatorNotes.put in: To put something in is to insert it, so I and SON go inside the copy.

annotation.surface: An artist at work puts a boy into an exact copy.
annotation.walkthrough: The accent on the final E is dropped in the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: this French enamelling technique, with colours set in wire cells, is a decorative art.

entries.clue: Established area covered by US phone briefly: it may give you a tinkle (7)

annotation.definition: it may give you a tinkle

indicatorNotes.covered by: In a down entry what covers something sits above it, so the phone piece comes first.
indicatorNotes.briefly: Briefly means in short, so the word loses its last letter.

blocks.note: CELL, the American word for a mobile phone, shortened

annotation.surface: A phone call from an American mobile.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Give you a tinkle' is British slang for phoning you, which the phone in the wordplay backs up; here it is a tinkling sound.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on slang: this keyboard instrument strikes metal plates and makes a bell-like tinkle.

entries.clue: Partner greeting king in conference (7)

annotation.surface: A partner greets the king at a summit.
annotation.walkthrough: Today the word more often means a fuss; the older sense is a parley.
annotation.definitionFit: An older sense: originally a long talk between traders and local people, hence a conference.

entries.clue: Lager, large tin, found in wharf (7)

indicatorNotes.found in: Something found in a place is inside it, so L and SN are inside the wharf.

blocks.note: a landing stage; LSN goes in after PI

annotation.surface: A big can of lager turns up on a wharf.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Large tin' reads as a big can of beer, but each word is a separate piece.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: this pale Czech-style beer is a type of lager.

entries.clue: Begin to understand how to date rays from the sun? (3,8)

annotation.definition2: how to date rays from the sun?

blocks.note: idiom for starting to grasp something at last

blocks.clueFragment: how to date rays from the sun?
blocks.note: to see someone is to date them; the sun's rays give light by day

annotation.surface: A whimsical question about courting sunshine.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half uses 'see' in its sense of going out with someone, applied to sunshine.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: an idiom for finally understanding, and literally dating the sun's light.

entries.clue: Going in just one direction, conserving energy for kicking (6)

indicatorNotes.conserving: To conserve is to keep safe, so TOING keeps the energy inside it.

blocks.note: the first half of 'toing and froing', going to without coming back
physics symbol; goes in after TO

annotation.surface: A footballer saving energy by only running one way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Toing and froing' means going back and forth, so its first half alone is going just one way.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain sense: striking a ball with the toe of the boot is a way of kicking.

entries.clue: Cart wife with angry words round shoe repairer (11)

indicatorNotes.round: Round means encircling, so W…ROW goes round the shoe repairer.

blocks.note: a heel bar is a small British shoe-repair counter

annotation.surface: A wife curses a cobbler.
annotation.walkthrough: A heel bar is a British kiosk, often in a station, that mends shoes while you wait.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a one-wheeled hand vehicle for loads is a kind of cart.

entries.clue: Lied in badly-written strong article to begin win (3-4)

indicatorNotes.badly-written: Something badly written has its letters wrong, so STRONG is rearranged.
indicatorNotes.to begin: To begin is to come first, so the article leads.

blocks.note: apparently a misprint for 'with' (the blog prints it the same way), making 'to begin with'

annotation.surface: A journalist lied in a sloppy, forceful piece.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lied' looks like the past tense of lie; it is the German word for song, said 'leed'.
annotation.definitionFit: A foreign word: a German Lied, as by Schubert, is a classical song for voice and piano.

entries.clue: Explorer yet to go west, south and as far as northeast (11)

blocks.note: to go west is to die, so one who has yet to is still alive

annotation.surface: An explorer who hasn't yet headed west, travelling south and up to the northeast.
annotation.walkthrough: The compass words all look like a route; 'go west' is the idiom for dying.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the Scottish missionary David Livingstone explored much of Africa.

entries.clue: Cutting to the quick with endlessly dazzling piece (11)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: Endlessly means without an end, so the last letter goes.

annotation.surface: A brilliant critique that stings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The quick' is an old word for the living, as in 'the quick and the dead'.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal rereading: surgery on live animals is cutting into the quick, the living.

entries.clue: Strongly protest as tormenter goes free (11)

indicatorNotes.goes free: Going free means breaking loose, so the letters break out of their order.

annotation.surface: A victim objects loudly when their abuser is released.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a courtroom outcry, which lands right beside the meaning of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to object forcefully and at length.

entries.clue: Close to bone in teaching, ignoring first instance of current assignment (11)

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' places the bone inside the word for teaching.
indicatorNotes.ignoring first instance of: To ignore is to leave out, and only the first of the two I's is left out.

blocks.note: one of the bones of the chest
physics symbol for electric current; dropping the first one leaves TUTION, with RIB going in after T

annotation.surface: A lesson on bones, skipping an electricity exercise.
annotation.walkthrough: TUITION has two I's; 'first instance' says which one goes.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: assigning credit or a cause to a source is attributing it.

entries.clue: Restaurant sent back article on large vessel (7)

indicatorNotes.sent back: Sent back means returned the way it came, so the string is read in reverse.

annotation.surface: A diner sends back a dish served on a big plate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sent back' is a restaurant complaint in the surface, and a turnaround signal in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a small Greek eating house is a kind of restaurant.

entries.clue: Searched roughly, carried out and dismissed (9)

blocks.note: managed, as in ran a project

annotation.surface: A burglary report: rooms searched, goods carried out, a guard fired.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carried out' reads as removing loot; it means conducted.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: going through a place violently and thoroughly.

entries.clue: Fine, though not hot, batter that’s used by cooks (3-6)

indicatorNotes.not: 'Though not hot' means without the H for hot, so that letter is removed.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, removed to leave TIN
a cricket batsman who starts the innings

annotation.surface: Cold batter is fine for cooking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Batter' looks like pancake mix beside 'cooks'; it is a cricketer.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by use: this kitchen tool, British for can opener, is used by cooks.

entries.clue: Quantity of work girl shoulders beginning to polish one large mirror (4,5)

indicatorNotes.shoulders: To shoulder something is to carry it on top, so in a down entry the girl comes below the rest.
indicatorNotes.beginning to: The beginning of a word is its first letter.

blocks.note: a unit of work in physics
a girl, especially in the north of England and Scotland

annotation.surface: A girl heaves a big mirror onto her shoulders to polish it.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down answer, a girl who shoulders things has them above her, so LASS comes last.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: this tall mirror hung between windows is a large looking-glass.

entries.clue: Having personal life publicised, raised voice angrily, wanting silence (5)

indicatorNotes.wanting: Wanting means lacking, so the word goes without the call for silence.

annotation.surface: Someone exposed in the press yells furiously and won't be hushed.
annotation.walkthrough: Removing the call for silence from a shout is the neat touch.
annotation.definitionFit: A modern idiom: someone whose private life, often their sexuality, has been made public without consent.

entries.clue: Cut off wickedness? I dither pathetically about it (10)

indicatorNotes.pathetically: Pathetically means feebly and badly, so the letters are feebly arranged.
indicatorNotes.about: About means surrounding, so the anagram goes round SIN.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters, which goes round SIN after DI
points back to 'wickedness', the thing the anagram goes about

annotation.surface: An indecisive parent wavers over punishing bad behaviour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It' refers back to 'wickedness', telling you what the anagram surrounds.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to cut someone off without a penny is to remove them from your will.

entries.clue: Trained horse always to skirt opening (7)

indicatorNotes.to skirt: To skirt is to pass round the edge, so E'ER goes round the outside of VENT.

blocks.note: an outlet or hole; it goes in after the first E

annotation.surface: A horse always shying round a gap in the hedge.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in the poetic contraction is dropped in the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a horse schooled for three-day eventing (dressage, cross-country, show jumping) is a trained horse.

entries.clue: Fixing of one series of races retrospectively stops trifling objections (12)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is usually an adjective; here it is the noun, the act of raising petty quibbles.

indicatorNotes.retrospectively: Retrospectively means looking back, so OF I TT is read backwards.
indicatorNotes.stops: To stop a hole is to plug it, so the reversed string plugs the middle of PEGGING.

blocks.note: the Isle of Man TT motorcycle races
fixing in place, as a price is pegged; TTIFO goes in after PE

annotation.surface: Race-fixing allegations put a stop to petty complaints.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fixing' reads as rigging races; it means holding in place. The TT is a road race on the Isle of Man.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain sense: quibbling over trivial details is making trifling objections.

entries.clue: Say, get sick of turning over leaves (7)

indicatorNotes.turning over: Turning something over flips it, so in a down entry the string runs bottom to top.

annotation.surface: Someone gets sick of turning pages.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as pages being turned; it is the plural of leaf.
annotation.definitionFit: A collective noun: a plant's leaves taken together.

entries.clue: Principals in ghastly armed robbery lost youthful looks in the lock-up (7)

indicatorNotes.Principals in: Principals are leaders, so the leading letters of the next three words are taken.

blocks.note: first letters of ghastly, armed, robbery

annotation.surface: The ringleaders of a robbery have grown old in jail.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lock-up' reads as a prison; it is a lock-up garage, where a car is kept.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on lock-up: a car kept in a rented garage is in the lock-up.

entries.clue: In disgusting housing a bachelor is OK to survive unaided (6)

indicatorNotes.housing: To house something is to give it a place inside, so VILE holds A B.

blocks.note: A plus B for bachelor; goes in after VI

annotation.surface: A bachelor in grim lodgings can still get by alone.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's bachelor fending for himself matches the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical sense: a foetus or seedling able to live independently is capable of surviving unaided.

entries.clue: Sheep-catching staff work with rope (7)

indicatorNotes.catching: To catch something is to take hold of it, so the staff holds the sheep inside.

blocks.note: a ceremonial rod of office; RAM goes in after MAC

annotation.surface: A shepherd uses a crook and rope to catch a sheep.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees; it is a rod.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: this craft of knotting cord into patterns is work with rope.

entries.clue: Laughs at exams (5)

blocks.note: practice exams sat in British schools before the real ones

annotation.surface: A student jeers at tests.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain, trial exams taken a few months before the real ones share this name.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a verb for ridiculing, and British school slang for practice exams.

entries.clue: Mangle words at first with one calling (7)

indicatorNotes.at first: At first means at the start, so the first letter is taken.

blocks.note: one who rings, on a phone or at a door

annotation.surface: An instruction to garble words when phoning.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mangle' reads as a verb, to garble; it is the noun, an old laundry machine.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a mangle is a pair of rollers for squeezing water from washing.

entries.clue: Physical laziness left feeling of annoyance we hear (7)

indicatorNotes.we hear: What we hear is sound, not spelling, so the piece is spelt differently from how it is said.

blocks.note: the feeling of being cross, spelt as in the answer

annotation.surface: Someone lazy is left feeling irritated.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is said 'lang-er', so L plus the annoyance sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a pleasant weariness or lack of physical energy.

entries.clue: Part of altercation at altar related to having children (5)

indicatorNotes.Part of: The answer is literally a part of the words that follow.

blocks.note: across the end of 'altercation', 'at' and the start of 'altar'

annotation.surface: A row at a wedding altar.
annotation.walkthrough: The wedding scene nods at the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to do with birth, as in antenatal classes.

entries.clue: Sportsman put off, missing start, following cramp (9)

indicatorNotes.missing start: Missing its start means without its first letter.
indicatorNotes.following: Following means coming after, so this piece comes after the cramp.

blocks.note: a painful stiffness, usually in the neck
discourage; missing its start gives ETER

annotation.surface: An athlete sidelined by a stiff neck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following' reverses the clue order, so the piece read first in the clue goes second.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a player of cricket is a sportsman.

entries.clue: Money a distant object for one worth nothing (5,8)

annotation.surface: For a penniless person, money is a distant dream.
annotation.walkthrough: A farthing was an old British coin worth a quarter of a penny; 'not a brass farthing' means nothing at all.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the proverbial coin of least value, standing for nothing at all.

entries.clue: Group of people fixed part of match (3)

blocks.note: a social circle, as in the jet-setters
fixed in place, as a time or price can be
a tennis match is divided into these

annotation.surface: A gang has rigged a game.
annotation.walkthrough: This is a triple definition: 'fixed' is a third meaning, which makes the surface read as match-fixing.
annotation.definitionFit: Three senses of one short word: a social circle, something fixed, and a unit of a tennis match.

entries.clue: Fellows receiving unknown backing for church meeting (5)

indicatorNotes.receiving: To receive is to take in, so the fellows take the unknown inside.
indicatorNotes.backing: Backing means moving backwards, so the result is read in reverse.

blocks.note: algebra's unknown; goes in after DON

annotation.surface: College fellows get anonymous support for a church assembly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads as support; here it turns the letters round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an assembly of clergy, and often laity, governing a church.

entries.clue: Put clothes back on for satisfaction (7)

blocks.note: to clothe oneself again: 'again' prefix plus 'clothe'
in the legal sense: amends for a wrong

annotation.surface: Getting dressed again feels satisfying.
annotation.walkthrough: Satisfaction here is the old sense of compensation, as when a duellist demanded satisfaction.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: dressing again, and the remedy owed for a grievance.

entries.clue: Like some avenues I entered, doubtful about length (4-5)

indicatorNotes.doubtful: Doubtful means uncertain, so the letters are in no settled order.
indicatorNotes.about: About means surrounding, so the anagram goes round the L.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation; sits inside the anagram

annotation.surface: Someone unsure how long an avenue was when they walked in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Entered' looks like the action in the surface; it is simply fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: many avenues have trees planted along both sides.
